title: Too Small to See, Still Alive

scenes.visual: Keep the existing silent title card.

scenes.tts: A drop of pond water can look completely clear. But tiny living things in that drop, an onion and you are all made of cells.
scenes.narration: A drop of pond water can look completely clear. But tiny living things in that drop, an onion and you are all made of cells.
scenes.caption: A drop of pond water can look completely clear. But tiny living things in that drop, an onion and you are all made of cells.
scenes.visual: Show a clear pond-water drop, then reveal tiny living things in a microscope inset. Place an onion and a person alongside it. Highlight cellular composition in all three; move immediately to the cell-theory scene.

scenes.tts: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life. The cell theory has three parts. All living things are made of one or more cells. The cell is the basic unit of life. All cells come from cells that already exist.
scenes.narration: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life. The cell theory has three parts. All living things are made of one or more cells. The cell is the basic unit of life. All cells come from cells that already exist.
scenes.caption: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life. The cell theory has three parts. All living things are made of one or more cells. The cell is the basic unit of life. All cells come from cells that already exist.
scenes.visual: Move this scene directly after the pond drop. Show one cell carrying the label smallest unit of life. Reveal three cards: living things made of one or more cells; cell as basic unit of life; an existing cell dividing into new cells. Keep all three statements visible together.

scenes.tts: Some organisms are just one cell. They are unicellular. A Paramecium in pond water is one cell. You and an oak tree are multicellular, made of many cells. Tiny does not always mean one cell. Some tiny pond animals have many cells.
scenes.narration: Some organisms are just one cell. They are unicellular. A Paramecium in pond water is one cell. You and an oak tree are multicellular, made of many cells. Tiny does not always mean one cell. Some tiny pond animals have many cells.
scenes.caption: Some organisms are just one cell. They are unicellular. A Paramecium in pond water is one cell. You and an oak tree are multicellular, made of many cells. Tiny does not always mean one cell. Some tiny pond animals have many cells.
scenes.visual: Compare one Paramecium, labelled unicellular, with a person and oak tree, labelled multicellular. Then show a tiny pond animal enlarged to reveal many cells. Do not imply every tiny pond organism is unicellular.

scenes.tts: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation backed by a great deal of evidence. The cell theory grew as better microscopes gave new evidence. Scientists found cells in many plants and animals. Some once thought new cells formed from clear fluid. More observations showed that new cells form when a cell divides. The theory dropped the wrong idea and kept the rest.

scenes.visual: Move this evidence scene ahead of the detailed microscope scenes. Show observations of plant and animal cells feeding into cell theory. Cross out the old clear-fluid formation idea and replace it with an existing cell dividing. End with the three theory cards supported by observations.

scenes.tts: Most cells are too small to see without help. Your eye can make out details down to about one hundred micrometres. A microscope uses lenses to make small things look larger. Magnification tells us how many times larger the image looks.
scenes.narration: Most cells are too small to see without help. Your eye can make out details down to about 100 micrometres. A microscope uses lenses to make small things look larger. Magnification tells us how many times larger the image looks.
scenes.caption: Most cells are too small to see without help. Your eye can make out details down to about 100 micrometres. A microscope uses lenses to make small things look larger. Magnification tells us how many times larger the image looks.
scenes.visual: Show most cells below the eye limit marked about 100 µm. Enlarge a sample through microscope lenses. Label the enlargement magnification. Remove the millimetre conversion sequence and the eyepiece-by-objective calculation.

scenes.tts: Seeing fine detail matters too. The best light microscopes show details down to about zero point two micrometres. A school microscope shows most whole cells. Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light. They showed cell parts too small for ordinary light microscopes.
scenes.narration: Seeing fine detail matters too. The best light microscopes show details down to about 0.2 micrometres. A school microscope shows most whole cells. Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light. They showed cell parts too small for ordinary light microscopes.
scenes.caption: Seeing fine detail matters too. The best light microscopes show details down to about 0.2 micrometres. A school microscope shows most whole cells. Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light. They showed cell parts too small for ordinary light microscopes.
scenes.visual: Distinguish enlarging an image from seeing fine detail. Mark the best light microscope detail limit at about 0.2 µm; show a school microscope revealing whole cells, then an electron microscope revealing finer cell parts. Do not depict enlargement alone as revealing new detail.

scenes.tts: Cells differ in shape and size, depending on their job and the organism they belong to. A red blood cell is a disc, pressed in on both faces. A nerve cell can have long, thin branches.

scenes.visual: Close with a red blood cell shown face-on and edge-on, then a nerve cell with long thin branches. Label shape and size depend on job and organism. Mark the comparison not to scale; omit exact cell dimensions.
